'''Sophie Geneviève Elisabeth Martin Benton''' is a Swiss biologist who is Professor and Director of the Department of Fundamental Microbiology at the [[University of Lausanne]].<ref name=gs>{{Google scholar id}}</ref><ref name=epmc>{{EuropePMC}}</ref> Her research investigates the molecular processes that underpin cellular fusion. She was awarded the [[EMBO Gold Medal]] in 2014.

== Early life and education ==
Martin was an undergraduate student at the [[University of Lausanne]], where she studied the organisation of chromatin with [[Susan M. Gasser]]. She was based in the [[Swiss Institute for Experimental Cancer Research]]. After graduating, Martin joined Daniel St Johnston at the [[University of Cambridge]], where she investigated the molecular mechanism of cell polarisation and the localisation of mRNA. She earned her PhD in 2002.<ref name=sophiephd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Cambridge|url=https://idiscover.lib.cam.ac.uk/permalink/f/t9gok8/44CAM_ALMA21432573770003606|doi=|title=Molecular and genetic analysis of cell polarisation, mRNA localisation and axis formation during Drosophila oogenesis|first= Sophie Geneviève|last=Martin|date=2002|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.620714}}|website=cam.ac.uk|oclc=894595744|hdl=}}</ref> 
  
== Research and career ==
Martin moved to [[Columbia University]], where she worked on cell polarisation and fission.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Prof. Sophie G Martin - AcademiaNet |url=https://www.academia-net.org/profil/prof-sophie-g-martin/1135365 |access-date=2022-07-18 |website=academia-net.org}}</ref> In 2007, Martin returned to the University of Lausanne, where she was made a [[Swiss National Science Foundation]] Professor at the Center for Integrative Genomics. She was promoted to full Professor in 2018.<ref name=g1>{{cite q|Q27936427}}</ref><ref name=g2>{{cite q|Q47946111}}</ref><ref name=g3>{{cite q|Q34530696}}</ref>

Martin was awarded a [[European Research Council]] Consolidator Grant to study cellular fusion.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Molecular dissection of the mechanisms of cell-cell fusion in the fission yeast |url=https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/681505 |website=cordis.europea.eu}}</ref> The fusion of cells is critical in fertilisation and development, and influences the formation of bone, tissue regeneration and cancer. Such fusion requires communication between cells, followed by polarisation, self-assembly and membrane juxtaposition.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The mechanisms of cell-cell fusion – The Martin Lab |url=https://wp.unil.ch/martinlab/research/the-mechanisms-of-cell-cell-fusion/ |access-date=2022-07-17 |language=en-US}}</ref> Her ERC Consolidator grant was focused on cellular fusion in ''[[Schizosaccharomyces pombe]]'', a simple yeast model. The cells are [[haploid]]s and fuse to form a diploid zygote. Martin studies the communication between cells and the mechanisms that underpin actin fusion focus formation.{{citation needed|date=July 2022}}
